case.label: D
case.text: Attaching the deny SCP directly to every member account also stops each account from leaving, so D meets the security goal; it loses only on overhead because each new account needs a manual attach, while one root attachment covers every current and future member account. C has no effect because SCPs do not restrict the management account, and B fails because the account administrators can edit their own IAM policies.

case.label: A
case.text: A candidate who thinks of AdministratorAccess as 'full power' could pick A, but an explicit Deny in an SCP is never overridden by an identity-based Allow; the only reason the call succeeds is that the principal is in the management account, which SCPs do not affect. The stem says 'in that account' clearly, so no second answer is defensible.

answers.flag: Every option grants only 'Athena actions', but Athena queries normally also call AWS Glue Data Catalog actions with the caller's credentials, so an allow-list SCP that allows only EC2, S3, CloudWatch and Athena may still block real Athena use; a careful candidate could call B (and A) incomplete, which an edit fixes by saying 'Athena and AWS Glue actions' or 'the actions that Athena needs'.

case.label: D
case.text: D looks attractive because the stem stresses that the account already has FullAWSAccess attached directly and the role allows Athena; a candidate who reads SCPs as additive at the account level would add an Athena SCP there. It fails because an action must be allowed by an SCP at every level from the root down to the account, and the Workloads OU allow list does not allow Athena. The detail 'has FullAWSAccess attached directly' is a deliberate lure toward D. A secondary concern for B: moving the account out of the Workloads OU also removes any other policies attached to that OU, which the stem does not mention.

case.label: A
case.text: Organizations plus StackSets with automatic deployment can also isolate environments, centralize logs and baseline future accounts, so A meets the functional requirements; it loses on overhead because the accounts, the log account and the baseline are built by hand. Option B does not name the log archive account explicitly, so a candidate who does not know that a landing zone sets up a dedicated log archive account could doubt B, but that is knowledge, not ambiguity.

case.label: E
case.text: A candidate could argue that each team owns its accounts, so each member account should activate the tag for its own report; in an organization, cost allocation tags are activated from the management account, so E is wrong. A further gap: activating a tag makes it available for cost allocation but does not by itself produce a 'monthly cost report for each team'; the stem accepts tag activation as the report step, and no other option does better, so the key still holds.

case.label: A
case.text: A candidate who remembers that invited accounts must approve the move to all features could link that approval to the role and pick A; but no Organizations action creates OrganizationAccountAccessRole in an invited account, so an administrator must create it by hand. D fails because SCPs do not restrict principals in the management account and the stem gives no such SCP.

case.label: C
case.text: C names the newer policy type and the familiar aws:PrincipalOrgID key, so a candidate who links 'S3 data protection' to RCPs could pick it; but an RCP on the company's root limits access to the company's own resources, not what the company's principals do on other organizations' buckets. The rule here is about the company's principals (an identity-side perimeter), so the SCP with aws:ResourceOrgID is the only option that applies to every current and future member account with one attachment. The stem says 'principals in the company's accounts must not access buckets that belong to other organizations' clearly, so no second answer is defensible; the twin q011 reverses the direction.

case.label: A
case.text: StackSets with automatic deployment to the OU would reach every new account without a change in how teams create accounts, while C depends on teams switching to Account Factory; a candidate could call A more 'automatic'. A still fails because Config rules are only detective and do not reproduce the preventive SCP-based controls, and it duplicates what Control Tower manages. C is the intended answer; registering the OU brings the OU-level controls to accounts placed in it.

answers.flag: Option C assumes that AWS Control Tower offers a preventive control that denies the deletion of the company's own named audit log buckets in the Workloads OU; the built-in preventive controls protect the resources that Control Tower itself creates, so a careful candidate could argue that only a custom SCP (option A, which certainly works, although it is attached per account) meets the requirement, and an edit should make clear that the control exists or offer a custom SCP attached to the OU.

case.label: A
case.text: A is a custom SCP that denies the deletion, so it is preventive, covers console and CLI, and works whether or not a matching Control Tower control exists; its only weakness is attaching to each account instead of the OU. If no ready-made Control Tower preventive control covers customer-defined buckets, C is not available and A becomes the correct answer. B is only detective (the stem rules out alerts), and D is proactive, which checks CloudFormation deployments and misses console and CLI changes, as the stem signals.

case.label: C
case.text: AWS RAM can share some resource types with IAM roles and users, so a candidate could pick C to share with the teams directly; subnets are shared with accounts, OUs or the organization, not with IAM roles, and the requirement that each team owns its instances in its own account points to account-level sharing. A fails ownership (the instances would belong to the network account) and D adds peering and route management that the stem wants to avoid.

case.label: D
case.text: A deny statement in every bucket policy does block outside principals, so D meets the security goal; it loses because teams create new buckets every week and each policy must be edited, and a bucket owner could remove the statement. The phrase 'even when a bucket policy allows them' cues a control above the bucket policy, which is the RCP. A practical nuance not in the stem: an RCP of this kind usually needs an exception for AWS service principals, but no option is affected by that.

case.label: D
case.text: Sharing with each account ID works without organization sharing, so D meets the immediate need; it fails the 'future accounts' requirement and adds invitations that each account must accept. A fails because SCPs never grant permissions, and C fails because Resolver rules are shared through AWS RAM, not with a hand-edited resource policy. The stem's detail that trusted access was turned on in the Organizations console points to the separate RAM setting, so B is the only fit.
